summary:
Kazakhstan decriminalised consensual sex between men in late 1997, when Article 104 of the Penal Code, which criminalised "buggery", was repealed; the repeal took effect in 1998 and introduced a common age of consent of 16. Sex between women was never a criminal offence. The sources record no statute regulating clothing by gender presentation and no law restricting which toilet or facility a trans visitor may use.

A statutory ban on "propaganda of non-traditional sexual orientation" is the operative legal threat. President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev signed the law on 30 December 2025, prohibiting "information containing propaganda of pedophilia and/or non-traditional sexual orientation" in public spaces and in the media, with violations punishable by a 10-day arrest and a fine. The Mäjilis had approved a harsher version on 12 November 2025. Kazakhstan now stands with Russia, Hungary and Georgia in prohibiting "LGBTQ propaganda" by law. This law followed a petition, "We Are against Open and Hidden LGBT Propaganda in Kazakhstan!" by the Union of Parents, which the Ministry of Culture and Information said in June 2024 it was reviewing after it met the threshold for government consideration; Human Rights Watch warned at the time that such a ban would violate rights nationwide.

Legal gender recognition on identity documents has been available since 2003, but only after a diagnosis of "gender identity disorder" involving medical tests and a 30-day psychiatric evaluation by a medical commission. Applicants must pay around ₸100,000 tenge. Since 2023 commissions can in principle be assembled in every region, but in practice the only functioning one is in Almaty, because of requirements for separate specialist rooms. A positive decision yields a certificate valid for six months to begin medical transition. Since 2011, document changes require gender-affirming surgery, hormone therapy and sterilisation; people under 21 cannot change gender on documents at all.

Same-sex couples cannot legally adopt; in February 2024 President Tokayev signed a law prohibiting adoption of orphans by same-sex couples, with the Deputy Minister of Education, Natalya Jumadildaeva, stating that a parent's sexual orientation would play a "key role" in approval, assessed through a "special psychological test". Critics, including independent media, noted the law was modelled on Russian legislation. Kazakhstan does not recognise same-sex marriage or civil unions, and same-sex couples and households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible to the same legal protections available to opposite-sex married couples. No laws exist protecting LGBTQ people from discrimination in employment, education, housing, health care, public accommodations or credit.

On documentation of bias violence, Kazakhstan has not reported hate-crime data to the OSCE/ODIHR since the 2018 report and has no nominated National Point of Contact for hate crimes; ODIHR's 2024 reporting notes the country would benefit from victim-support and awareness measures. ILGA-Europe's Annual Review for January–December 2023 records an LGBTQI+ education NGO denied employment-site registration after listing its focus, and an LGBTQI activist almost run over with no investigation opened. The same review documents a wave of transgender people arriving from Russia since 2022. Human Rights Watch reported on 24 September 2019 that Kazakhstan's Supreme Court ordered compensation from a Facebook user who posted a video of two women kissing and solicited homophobic comments, upholding privacy rights over a "moral foundations" defence; the women fled Kazakhstan for eight months fearing for their safety. ECOM, which has monitored and documented rights violations against LGBT people since 2017, identifies health-right barriers in Kazakhstan alongside informal behavioural practices that policy analysis misses.
tangentialFactors:
Public opinion is a background factor: 89% of people opposed same-sex marriage in a 2015–16 Pew survey. The figure is a decade old and measures attitudes toward marriage, not current behaviour toward trans visitors.

The 2025 propaganda law places Kazakhstan alongside Russia, Hungary and Georgia in prohibiting "LGBTQ propaganda" by law, a regional pattern that shapes how a trans visitor's visibility in public space may be treated.

The institutional gap in hate-crime documentation means that bias violence against a trans visitor may go unrecorded: no hate-crime data has been reported to ODIHR since 2018 and there is no nominated National Point of Contact.

outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no region-specific signal for Kazakhstan's sub-national units beyond the note that the only functioning gender-recognition commission sits in Almaty; the national assessment applies.

No source in this inventory documents a trans-specific killing or violence rate for Kazakhstan against which a general homicide rate could be compared, so no such figure is stated. The 2023 ILGA-Europe entry records one activist almost run over with no investigation, a single documented incident rather than a prevalence measure.

The 89% figure on same-sex marriage opposition comes from a 2015–16 Pew survey and is dated; it measures attitudes toward marriage, not current trans-specific risk.

Whether the 2025 propaganda law has been enforced against trans expression specifically, and how the Almaty-only commission requirement affects applicants outside Almaty in practice, are not resolved by these sources.
